theme: The shadow vs. the reality; the new and living way
readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 10:1-39. Notice the shift from argument to exhortation around verse 19. The first half completes the case that Christ’s sacrifice is final. The second half draws three “let us” conclusions for how to live. Pay attention to verses 26-31, which are sobering, and verses 32-39, which are full of encouragement.
settingTheScene: The author has spent several chapters building his case for the better priest, better covenant, and better sacrifice. Chapter 10 brings the argument to its climax and then turns on a hinge into the application. The first section returns to the idea of shadow and reality, and the second part invites readers to enter by the new and living way. Throughout, there is a pastoral concern. These Christians had faced hostility and lost property. They were tempted to withdraw. The author wants them to see that the cost of leaving Christ is far greater than the cost of staying.
observation: The law has “a shadow of the good things to come,” not the true form of these realities (10:1).
If animal sacrifices could cleanse, they would have stopped. Instead they are “a reminder of sins every year” (10:2-3).
“It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (10:4).
Psalm 40:6-8 is quoted as the words of Christ: “a body have you prepared for me… Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (10:5-7).
“By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (10:14).
We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (10:19-20).
Three exhortations follow: “let us draw near,” “let us hold fast,” and “let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (10:22-24).
“We are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls” (10:39).
interpretation:
The opening of chapter 10 distills the argument. The law offered a shadow, not the image itself. If the sacrifices of the Day of Atonement could have perfected the worshipers, they would have been offered no more. But the very repetition showed their limitation. Each year the people were reminded of their sins, because the blood of bulls and goats could not take sin away.

Then comes the voice of Christ in Psalm 40. The Son speaks to the Father at the moment of the incarnation: sacrifices and offerings you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me. “Behold, I have come to do your will.” The will of God is that we be sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. This is the center of the chapter. A body was prepared so that a sacrifice could be made that actually works.

The contrast between the standing priests and the seated Christ is the author’s recurring image. Every priest stands daily, offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins. But Christ, having offered a single sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down. And because of that single offering, he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Notice the tenses. The perfection is complete, and the sanctification is ongoing. Believers are already fully cleansed in their standing and are still being made holy in their experience. The new covenant promise is repeated: “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” And where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin.

Now the hinge. Verses 19-25 begin with “therefore” and turn argument into invitation. The curtain that separated humanity from God’s presence has been opened through Christ’s flesh. In the temple, the curtain was torn from top to bottom at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:51), and the author uses this image: the curtain is his flesh. We can enter with confidence, with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water. The three exhortations follow: draw near in faith, hold fast the confession of hope without wavering, and stir one another up to love and good works, “not neglecting to meet together.”

Verses 26-31 are among the most sobering in the New Testament. If we deliberately go on sinning after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice remains. The author is describing those who persistently reject Christ and treat his blood as common. To spurn the Son is a more serious offense than breaking the law of Moses. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” The point is not to undermine assurance but to underline how much is at stake.

But he ends with encouragement. He reminds them of their former courage: they endured a hard struggle, were publicly exposed to reproach, and joyfully accepted the plundering of their property, since they knew they had a better and abiding possession. He tells them not to throw away their confidence. “For you have need of endurance.” The one who is coming will come and will not delay. “The righteous shall live by faith.” And then comes the closing assurance: “We are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.”
connection: This chapter quotes Psalm 40 (Day 824), Jeremiah 31 (Day 828), Deuteronomy 32:35-36, and Habakkuk 2:3-4. The “new and living way” through the curtain links to Exodus 26:31-33, where the veil separated the holy place from the most holy place, and to the tearing of the veil in Matthew 27:51. Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11. The call to meet together prepares for the next day’s doctrinal reading.
application:
First, accept the invitation. You have confidence to enter God’s presence by the blood of Jesus. If you have been treating prayer as a duty or a risk, remember that the way is open.

Second, examine your commitment to gathering with the church. Verse 25 does not treat attendance as optional. Ask who in your church needs your encouragement, and make a plan to talk to them this week.

Third, think about endurance. The original readers had lost property for Christ. What have you been willing to lose? What have you been unwilling to risk? Ask the Lord for courage.

Fourth, take verse 38 as a daily motto: the righteous shall live by faith.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for opening the way through the curtain by his body.
Draw near with a true heart in full assurance, and tell him so.
Ask him to help you hold fast and encourage others.
